gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1031t:
Managerial Cost Accounting Practices: Departments of Labor and Veterans Affairs. GAO-05-1031T of September 21, 2005, is the spoken form of a study on how two big departments count the cost of their work. A web of laws, among them the Federal Financial Management Improvement Act of 1996, tells agencies to build true cost data. Chiefs then use that data to steer plans and answer for results.

GAO briefed staff on July 15, 2005, and put its full findings out on September 2, 2005. The statement tells how Labor and Veterans Affairs build their cost counts. It tells how chiefs there put the counts to use, and where the craft fell short.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1041t:
VA Health Care, GAO-05-1041T of September 26, 2005, shares early findings on a plan to build a joint medical center in Charleston. The Medical University of South Carolina put the plan to the Department of Veterans Affairs in 2002. Both sides would build and run one new center on the school's growing campus. A 2004 review panel urged VA to judge the plan fast.

GAO checked three things so far. It checked the state of the old Charleston site. It checked how well VA and the school worked as a team. It checked what VA must weigh before it signs on. VA agreed with the early findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-1051t:
Computer-Based Patient Records, GAO-05-1051T of September 28, 2005, updates a 7-year push to let two departments swap patient files by computer. The Departments of Veterans Affairs and Defense each run vast health systems. A shared file would ease the move from active duty to veteran life. It would also back care and disability claims with full facts.

GAO checks near-term steps to swap data on the old systems. It checks the long goal too: new systems that talk both ways. Gains are real, the title grants. Much work still stands between the two networks and a true shared record for each patient.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-321t:
Financial Management, GAO-05-321T of February 16, 2005, makes the case that tight inner checks are the base of trust in government. Checks on cash, facts, and work steps show if funds go where law sends them. Congress has kept a long watch on this craft. The budget office had just reshaped its rule book for checks, called Circular A-123.

GAO tells what two decades of agency grades have taught. It gives its view of the new rules. Six needs stand out. They are clear guides and tools, care for more than cash checks, and chiefs who back the work at each tier. The rest are fair cost for gain, true tests, and blame when checks break.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-361t:
Telecommunications, GAO-05-361T of March 3, 2005, gives a progress note on a vast new phone and net buy for the whole state. The Networx plan, first sketched in October 2003, would take the place of deals set to lapse. One arm would give full voice and data reach, land-wide and world-wide. One arm would give net-based tools with less reach. A draft ask went out in October 2004.

Trade and agency views on that draft topped 2,500 notes. GAO had urged fixes in September 2004, on the move plan, feat marks, and bills. Gains stand in the new plan work, it finds. Key points still wait for a call.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-391t:
Human Capital, GAO-05-391T of March 2, 2005, gives GAO's read of the final rules for a new staff system at the homeland arm. Congress let the Department of Homeland Security draw its own rules for pay, feats, blame, and union ties. The aim was a swift, feat-based craft. Staff are the arm's core wealth, GAO notes. Rules shape how that wealth is won and kept.

Last year, GAO found the draft rules in line with sound craft in the main. Hard points sat in pay, blame paths, and union ties. The facts here grade the final rules on those points. It flags the strain of the launch to come.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-401t:
Federal Mandates, GAO-05-401T of March 8, 2005, rests on a May 12, 2004 report on a law that guards towns and states from unfunded orders. The Unfunded Mandate Reform Act of 1995 came from fears that Washington sets tasks and leaves the bill. In the 10 years since, Congress has weighed tweaks to the act more than once. What counts as such an order is the crux.

The facts here tell how an order gets flagged as one. They tell what part each agency plays in that hunt. They list laws and rules that met the bar. They list some that miss the bar in law but feel like orders to those who pay.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-431t:
Handing security duties to Iraqi military and police forces is covered in GAO testimony GAO-05-431T, dated March 14, 2005. The United States had given about $5.8 billion in 2003 and 2004 to build Iraqi security forces. A further $5.7 billion was requested in February 2005. GAO gave early views on the transfer strategy, the data on force status, and the problems the multinational force faced.

A transfer strategy existed and was being put into effect. But reported force numbers were not reliable. The State Department cited about 82,000 trained police and almost 60,000 trained military personnel. Police counts missed men absent from duty, and reporting from around the country was uneven. Data on weapons, vehicles, and body armor were no longer reported. Attacks had also grown in number and force since June 2003. The testimony flags four problems, from training a changing force to judging readiness.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-561t:
The tax-exempt sector and its oversight are surveyed in testimony GAO-05-561T, given on April 20, 2005. More than a million and a half groups hold exempt status under section 501(c) of the tax code. Their stated assets passed $2.5 trillion by 2002. The sector's spending equals about one tenth of the economy. GAO addressed its growth, the part played by good governance and openness, and the watch kept by the IRS and the states.

Sound boards and open books help exempt groups stay honest and on mission, GAO said.   The IRS, though, has struggled to keep up. Staffing trends and poor data have limited its reach. It has begun to add staff and better data tools, and it runs special drives on the worst compliance problems. States police charities as well, often guarding donors and assets. GAO said trust in the sector rests on all of these layers working.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-571t:
The budget office's watch list for troubled technology projects is the topic of testimony GAO-05-571T, presented on April 21, 2005. Federal technology spending tops $60 billion this year. Of 1,200 major projects in the fiscal year 2005 budget, the office flagged 621 as needing management fixes. Those projects carry about $22 billion. GAO reported on how the list is built and how fixes ordered for listed projects are followed up.

The office set rules for scoring project plans and used them to spot weak ones. But it never built one combined list of the flagged projects and their faults. Each analyst kept the list for a few agencies. The total of 621 came from polling those analysts.  Follow-up on fixes was also uneven. No set process decided how closely each fix would be watched. GAO said the watch list could do far more as a tool for spotting government-wide patterns.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-631t:
Chemical plant security after the terror attacks is covered by GAO-05-631T, testimony of April 27, 2005. About 15,000 sites hold large stocks of the most dangerous chemicals. Experts rank them among the most tempting targets: a toxic release could sicken crowds and stall trade. By 2003 data, 123 plants had worst cases putting over a million people within reach of a gas cloud.

Only about one-sixth of the sites face federal security rules. Some 2,000 water systems and 238 waterside plants must check their weak points. No one has yet surveyed safety at all the plants, GAO notes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-651t:
The Coast Guard's aging deepwater fleet anchors GAO testimony GAO-05-651T (June 21, 2005). A replacement program begun in 2002 may cost $19 billion to $24 billion. The old cutters and aircraft are wearing out, but the service's own gauges cannot say how badly. Visits by GAO found faults across many systems. Crews patch the gap with heavier upkeep between voyages, yet ships still lose mission capacity. One scheme to nurse the oldest cutters needs money no budget seeks.

Speeding up replacement adds risk. GAO questions the plan to let one prime contractor design and deliver the whole fleet.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-741t:
In testimony GAO-05-741T (May 24, 2005), GAO reported on federal work to use woody biomass. Crews thin forests to cut wildfire risk. The work leaves piles of small trees, limbs, and brush. This material has little market value now. GAO named the agencies involved, how they coordinate, and what blocks wider use.

GAO found most work sits with the Agriculture, Energy, and Interior departments. They give grants, run research, and teach users about the material. Two joint groups help the agencies coordinate. Day-to-day contact, though, is mostly informal. Staff named hard blocks, led by cost and weak markets. The testimony rests on a full GAO report issued at the same time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-761t:
Amtrak's food and drink service is dissected in testimony GAO-05-761T, dated June 9, 2005. Amtrak has sold food on its trains since 1971. The service loses money year after year. GAO used it as a window on wider cost control at Amtrak. It checked the contract with the firm that runs dining stock, and the checks Amtrak keeps on costs.

GAO found that Amtrak spends about $2 for each $1 the service earns. Losses came to almost $245 million from fiscal years 2002 through 2004. The contract pays the firm's costs plus fees, which gives it little reason to cut costs. Amtrak also failed to use five key controls in full. Those gaps include audits of bills and of discounts owed.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-811t:
A vast visitor center under the Capitol is tracked in testimony GAO-05-811T, given June 14, 2005. The Architect of the Capitol runs the build. Congress last heard an update on May 17. GAO checked progress on set milestones since then. It reviewed schedules and money reports, visited the site, and spoke with project staff. The work was done to aid oversight, GAO noted, not as a full audit.

The testimony lays out where the schedule stands and what slippage could do to costs. Funding levels and gaps are covered in detail. GAO's message matches its title. The project needs tighter schedule management. It also needs cost figures that are updated and shared in the open. Readers get a snapshot of a major public build at a tense point.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-841t:
AIDS funding formulas are probed in testimony GAO-05-841T, presented June 23, 2005. A 1990 law funds care for people living with HIV and AIDS. Over $2 billion flowed through it in fiscal year 2004. Most money goes by formula to big city areas and to states. The formulas rest on counts of AIDS cases. Drug help programs sit inside the state grants.

GAO gave early findings on four questions. How do case-based formulas shape who gets what? How do limits on yearly cuts affect the spread? What shifts would follow if HIV counts joined AIDS counts in the math? And how do state drug programs differ in who qualifies and what funds them? The testimony frames a debate over whether the formulas track the epidemic as it now stands.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-861t:
A small business research program is recalled in testimony GAO-05-861T, given June 28, 2005. The program dates to 1982. It steers federal research money to small, inventive firms. GAO has reviewed it many times over the years. This statement sums up its record of success. It also names the one challenge that has stayed unresolved for nearly two decades.

Between July 1985 and June 1999, GAO reported on the program again and again. It generally found the program meets its goals. Agencies and firms rated it highly. Weak spots included duplicate funding of like projects and clashing readings of research budgets. Awards also clustered in a few states. Most GAO fixes were adopted in law or by agencies. How to judge the program's long-term results remains open, GAO said.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-891t:
Space buying problems are diagnosed in testimony GAO-05-891T, delivered July 12, 2005. GAO drew on years of reports on defense space systems. It covered the causes of failure, the pressures behind them, and possible fixes. The pattern across most big space programs was the starting point.

GAO found the results discouraging. Systems cost more and take much longer than promised at approval. In some cases, the case for the system itself had to be rethought. The root flaw is a mismatch set at the start. Requirements are vague or shift midstream. Technologies enter development before they are mature. Cost estimates rest on those unknowns, so they prove unreliable. GAO urged stronger development practice and investment planning.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-911t:
Pricing on government buying schedules is examined in testimony GAO-05-911T, given July 26, 2005. Agencies buy over $32 billion a year in goods and services this way. More than 16,000 contracts list over 8 million products. The buying agency must win discounts at least as good as a vendor's best customer gets. GAO focused on two audit tools meant to keep prices honest.

GAO found the tools are used only now and then. Audits before award can stop overpricing. Audits after award can claw back overcharges. In the early 1990s, both were used well: nearly $480 million saved in talks and about $90 million recovered in 5 years. A 1997 rule change ended the after-award audits in practice. Before-award audits never grew to fill the gap. One contract alone was set to overcharge buyers by nearly $40 million, an inspector general found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1071t:
A national health IT strategy gets a progress note in testimony GAO-06-1071T, given September 1, 2006. In April 2004, the President called for linked electronic health records within 10 years. A national coordinator was named the next month. A framework for action followed two months later. In May 2005, GAO urged detailed plans and milestones for each phase. This testimony reports progress since.

Headings chart the work. The health department continues efforts to finish and carry out a national strategy. It is advancing use of electronic records. It has begun steps on shared standards and on requirements for a national network. Privacy and security policy work is under way. Public health links are also being addressed. The testimony gives Congress the state of each strand in one account.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1091t:
A strong safety record, strained by growth, frames GAO-06-1091T, testimony given in September 2006. Traffic will rise, and unmanned craft and very light jets will enter shared airspace. GAO asked how the Federal Aviation Administration targets the highest risks. It also asked whether FAA staff keep the skills for steady oversight. The statement draws on recent GAO reports and industry talks.

FAA aims inspection staff at areas of greatest risk through a system safety approach. Outside designees perform about 90 percent of certification tasks, freeing FAA staff. Yet GAO found weak spots in program data and result checks. Inspector training mostly followed good practice, but some steps lagged. Past recommendations call for better data, real program reviews, and more designee training. FAA has begun that work, though much remains unfinished.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-1121t:
Free tutoring under the No Child Left Behind Act is examined in GAO-06-1121T, testimony dated September 21, 2006. Schools that miss state goals for three straight years must offer low-income students extra help, called supplemental educational services. The statement rests on GAO's August 2006 report on the program. GAO surveyed states and districts, visited four districts, and spoke with tutoring providers. It tracked how many students took part and how the services were run.

The testimony covers how participation shifted in recent years. It explains how providers work with districts to deliver tutoring. It also reviews how states watch and grade the services, and how the Department of Education supports them. Early rollout raised hard questions about sign-ups, quality checks, and proof that tutoring lifts achievement. The statement gives lawmakers an early read on a program meant to help students in struggling schools.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-181t:
Passenger rail security after the London bombings is the focus of GAO-06-181T, testimony from October 2005. The July 2005 attacks on London's subway showed how open rail systems are to terror strikes. GAO reviewed how the Department of Homeland Security grades rail risks. It covered steps federal agencies have taken to harden U.S. rail systems. It also compared security habits of U.S. and foreign rail operators.

Two units inside the department run risk reviews, but their work is not yet joined up. The security agency has not finished its method for ranking rail risks. Without it, the agency cannot set clear investment priorities. A department-wide frame for comparing risks across sectors is also unfinished. Rail operators at home and abroad use guards, cameras, and rider awareness drives. Some foreign systems also screen riders at random and test staff in secret. GAO urged stronger federal leadership to set priorities.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-201t:
The chief information officer's role at the Department of Veterans Affairs is discussed in GAO-06-201T, testimony from October 2005. The department leans hard on technology and sought about $2.1 billion for it in fiscal year 2006. A 1996 law made the CIO the focal point for agency tech management. GAO compared CIO duties in government and in top private firms. It traced how the VA post has grown over time, drawing on a 2004 federal study and a 2005 private-sector study.

The two worlds look much alike, GAO found. Federal and private CIOs carry near-equal shares of most duties. Both cite the same hard problems: weak processes, scarce tech leaders, and system security. At VA, years of acting or part-time CIOs ended with a full-time appointment in August 2001. In 2002 the department moved to centralize tech control under the CIO. GAO saw promise in that shift for clearer accountability.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-221t:
Lessons from a flu vaccine shortage shape GAO-06-221T, testimony presented on November 4, 2005. Fear of a flu pandemic has grown, and vaccine supply is a weak point. In October 2004 one of two big makers pulled its whole supply. The nation lost about half its expected flu vaccine for that season. GAO studied how federal, state, and local bodies coped. The statement draws on its September 2005 report on the shortage and past work on pandemic planning.

The scramble showed what a pandemic would demand. Officials had to ration scarce shots, calm the public, and hunt new supply at speed. Those tasks grow far harder in a global outbreak. GAO sets out the lessons the shortfall taught. It ties them to plans for future seasons and for a pandemic. The testimony is a case study in how a supply shock tests the whole health system.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-251t:
A month later, GAO returned to Congress on the Capitol Visitor Center in GAO-06-251T, testimony dated November 16, 2005. This update picks up the story from the October 18 hearing. It covers three threads: the build schedule, cost and funding, and worker safety. Work on site moved ahead in parts. The task of building one stable master schedule lagged behind the physical work. That gap limits what anyone can promise about the finish date.

GAO again held off on naming a completion date. The Architect of the Capitol and its construction manager had not finished their schedule reviews. Until the schedule firms up, cost forecasts stay soft. GAO updated cost and funding facts from data at hand. It saved its full cost-to-complete update for a stable schedule. The testimony is one chapter in a long oversight serial on a troubled build. It shows why schedule truth comes before cost truth.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-281t:
Why health care prices swing from city to city is explored in GAO-06-281T, testimony presented on December 2, 2005. Use of care across regions is well mapped; price gaps are less known. Spending equals use times price, so price gaps matter. GAO drew on its August 2005 study of claims in the federal workers' health program. That study found wide price gaps across metro areas. The gaps held after adjusting for local costs and the mix of care. This statement digs into what drives them.

Competition plays a clear role, GAO found. Where fewer hospitals or doctor groups compete, prices tend to run higher. Other local factors add to the spread. The statement also weighs how much of the regional spending gap comes from price rather than volume. Market structure shapes the bill before any care is given. The testimony gives Congress a price lens on health spending.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-371t:
Airport screening had grown stronger, yet weak spots stayed. In testimony GAO-06-371T (April 4, 2006), GAO reports on passenger and checked baggage screening. The Transportation Security Administration had run screening for over three years. Hundreds of airports and thousands of flights made the task huge. Millions of passengers and bags moved through each day.

GAO tracked gains in the screener workforce. It covered hiring, training, and placement of officers. It also checked screening steps and new technology. The testimony credits real enhancements. It also warns that challenges remain. Readers see where screening improved and where it lagged. The focus stays on safety in daily use.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-481t:
Dust and trauma from a collapsed tower shadowed responders for years. The testimony numbered GAO-06-481T, delivered February 28, 2006, updates health monitoring after the World Trade Center attack. Nearly 3,000 people died in the 2001 attack. An estimated 250,000 to 400,000 people nearby were affected. About 40,000 responders were exposed to physical and mental health hazards. Several federally funded programs track those effects.

GAO assessed programs run by state, local, and private groups. It also reviewed federal programs for federal responders. Monitoring has progressed, GAO said. The program for federal responders lags behind, it added. The statement also draws lessons for future disasters. It updates a briefing from September 10, 2005.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-531t:
Sensitive but unclassified papers need marks that staff apply the same way. Testimony GAO-06-531T, dated March 14, 2006, returns to managing sensitive information. The Energy Department marks such material Official Use Only. The Defense Department uses For Official Use Only. Both marks limit sharing for security, privacy, and other reasons. This statement presents the same study as a companion report.

GAO compares the rules, steps, and criteria each department uses. It judges training and oversight meant to ensure correct marking. Both departments could improve their policies and oversight, GAO said. Readers who want the short form of the study will find it here. The testimony format is the difference.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-561t:
This statement carries a disability study to a House military panel. Testimony GAO-06-561T, given April 6, 2006, presents GAO's recent study of military disability evaluation. The House Subcommittee on Military Personnel asked for the briefing. The study compares Defense policies for the Army, Navy, and Air Force. It notes rules specific to reserve members. It also reviews oversight and quality controls in place.

GAO compared Army decisions, ratings, and processing times for active and reserve members. The Army is the largest branch. The statement seeks consistent and timely outcomes, as its title says. Readers get the study's questions and design in short form. Findings mirror the companion report.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-581t:
A second April statement returns to improper payments, with the same core questions. Testimony GAO-06-581T, given April 5, 2006, reports agency progress under the Improper Payments Information Act of 2002. Fiscal year 2005 was the second year of required reports. Agencies must identify programs prone to significant improper payments. They must estimate amounts and report actions to reduce them. Those reports appear in yearly performance and accountability reports.

GAO looked at how far agencies performed risk assessments. It reports the yearly amount of improper payments estimated. It also tracked sums recouped through recovery audits. Challenges continue, GAO said. Readers can set this statement beside the March version for the update.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-591t:
A computer model helps officers pick which cargo containers to open. Testimony GAO-06-591T, dated March 30, 2006, gives early observations on the Automated Targeting System. Customs and Border Protection uses the system to target oceangoing containers for inspection. It forms part of a layered approach to cargo security. GAO reported in February 2004 on challenges in that targeting. It made recommendations on modeling practice and on updating the strategy. This statement reports early results from follow-up work.

GAO asks what controls assure the system targets the highest-risk containers. It checks how inspection results feed back into the model. It also reviews steps to improve the wider targeting strategy at seaports. The observations are preliminary.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-601t:
Congress can strike down agency rules, and the tool turned ten years old. Testimony GAO-06-601T, given March 30, 2006, marks ten years of the Congressional Review Act. Oversight of rulemaking through the act can help monitor the regulatory process. It balances concerns of citizens and businesses with the effects of agency rules. The statement gives an overview of the act's purpose and terms. It explains GAO's role under the act.

GAO also sets out trends in use of the act. Those trends sit within wider shifts in presidential and congressional oversight. Readers get a compact history of a check on the regulatory state. The anniversary framing is explicit in the text.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-631t:
Park Service funding trends are laid out in GAO-06-631T, testimony GAO delivered on April 5, 2006. The statement covers fiscal years 2001 through 2005, a period when advocacy groups questioned whether parks had enough money to run well. GAO tracked the main operations account and visitor fees. GAO also looked closely at 12 busy park units and how funding shifts affected their daily work.

GAO found that appropriations rose from about $1.4 billion in fiscal year 2001 to almost $1.7 billion in fiscal year 2005. That growth averaged about 5 percent a year, or about 1 percent after inflation. Yet the share set aside for daily operations fell slightly in real terms, while project funds grew. GAO also reviewed new steps the Park Service took to track spending and results.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-681t:
AIDS drug aid and HIV prevention are covered together in GAO-06-681T, testimony GAO presented on April 26, 2006. The testimony draws on GAO's review of AIDS Drug Assistance Programs under the Ryan White CARE Act. These state programs buy HIV drugs for people who cannot afford them. The testimony also addresses efforts to stop mother-to-child spread of HIV and to notify partners of infected persons.

GAO reported that differences in program design and funding led to wide variation in who and what each program covered. Some programs paid prices above a federal discount benchmark for selected drugs. The federal agency in charge did not routinely compare program prices against that benchmark. GAO also found that the benchmark price topped other federal prices for some drugs. The findings fed a debate on reauthorizing the act.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-701t:
Oversight inside the United Nations is the topic of GAO-06-701T, testimony GAO gave on April 27, 2006. Scandals in UN programs had raised doubts about how the world body polices itself. GAO reviewed the UN's internal oversight office and its procurement controls. Procurement is the path through which billions flow to vendors for peacekeeping and relief work. Weak vendor screening can invite fraud and poor performance.

GAO told the House panel that oversight and procurement controls needed strengthening. The UN did not consistently follow its own process for checking that vendors were qualified. GAO set out recommendations to tighten both areas. The testimony reflects United States pressure for reform at the UN. It also lists the control steps GAO viewed as most urgent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-711t:
The UN Oil for Food program is revisited in GAO-06-711T, testimony presented on May 2, 2006. Sanctions on Iraq began in 1990, and the program started in 1996. It let Iraq sell oil to pay for humanitarian goods while blocking military items. More than $67 billion in oil revenue flowed through the program. Some $31 billion in assistance reached Iraq. Later probes found corruption and smuggling on a large scale.

GAO drew lessons for future sanctions and for UN reform. Lines of responsibility in the program were unclear, and risk was not tracked over time. Oil export monitoring did not deter smuggling. The UN internal audit office lacked enough resources and independence. GAO said clearer authority and stronger audit capacity are key fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-761t:
Long-term budget trouble and the process that feeds it fill GAO-06-761T, testimony GAO gave on May 25, 2006. GAO called the nation's long-term fiscal outlook daunting. The budget process did not cause the problem by itself. But the lack of real budget controls and other guardrails had made the challenge worse. A better process could shine light on looming costs and reward wiser choices.

GAO urged more transparency about long-term costs in budget debates. It also backed stronger controls, plus triggers and default rules that act when targets are missed. Such mechanisms would push lawmakers to face hard trade-offs sooner. The testimony is a plea to fix the rules of budgeting before the fiscal gap grows beyond easy repair. It reflects GAO's standing fiscal warning to Congress.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-801t:
Management at the crash investigation agency is assessed in GAO-06-801T, testimony GAO gave on May 24, 2006. The National Transportation Safety Board is small, with about 400 staff and a budget of $76.7 million in fiscal year 2006. Yet it holds a worldwide name for probing transport accidents. GAO shared early observations on its planning and practices. GAO also weighed the value of its training academy for investigators.

GAO found a mixed record on leading management practices. The board had hired a chief financial officer and put controls on purchasing. Those steps should curb past problems with unapproved buys. But the board lacked a full cost accounting system to show what its work consumes. GAO said fuller planning and wider use of proven practices would strengthen the agency. Its academy, GAO noted, is an asset worth using more.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-851t:
Corporate tax enforcement and stock sale reporting meet in GAO-06-851T, testimony GAO presented on June 13, 2006. When investors sell securities, they must report capital gains or losses to the tax agency. Many get the math wrong, because the original cost of the asset, its basis, is easy to lose or misstate. GAO summarized its findings on these errors and on the wider challenges of corporate tax enforcement.

GAO found that many taxpayers misreport capital gains or losses. Some underpay their taxes as a result, while others overpay. The revenue service has efforts in place to improve reporting, but they face several obstacles. GAO said wider third-party reporting of asset basis could help. Brokers would report the cost data directly. The testimony weighs that fix against the burden it would add.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-861t:
The personnel agency's own reform capacity is the topic of GAO-06-861T, testimony GAO presented on June 27, 2006. The Office of Personnel Management leads human capital policy for the whole government. Reform plans would have it guide agencies and certify their readiness for new personnel systems. To play that role, the office must first build its own internal strength. GAO reported on the steps it was taking.

GAO said the office was working on its leadership bench and its talent base. It had engaged in workforce planning for its own staff. Those steps aim to give the office the experts it needs to advise others. GAO viewed the effort as under way, not complete. The testimony frames a simple point: the agency that grades reform must first pass its own test.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-871t:
Invasive forest pests at the border are the focus of GAO-06-871T, testimony GAO presented on June 21, 2006. Foreign beetles and fungi have seriously harmed United States forests and cost the economy heavily. The Agriculture Department leads the response, working with the Homeland Security Department at ports of entry. GAO had issued two reports on these programs in 2006. This testimony sums up the state of three major infestations.

GAO reported that the fight against the Asian longhorned beetle looks likely to succeed. That pest holds small areas in Illinois, New Jersey, and New York. The outlook is darker for the emerald ash borer and the sudden oak death pathogen. Both infest far wider areas and resist eradication. GAO warned that weak points at ports keep forests at risk. Prevention at entry, GAO implied, is the cheapest cure.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-901t:
Oversight of the H-1B visa program by the Department of Labor is examined in GAO testimony GAO-06-901T, dated June 22, 2006. The program lets U.S. firms hire skilled foreign workers for a set term. Labor shares program duties with Homeland Security and Justice.

The testimony sums up GAO report GAO-06-720. That work told how Labor carries out its H-1B duties on the ground. It also told how Labor works with the other agencies in the program. GAO urged Labor to improve checks of employer papers. Readers get a compact view of how a major work visa is policed, and where gaps sit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-961t:
Industrial loan corporations, a fast-growing kind of lender, are profiled in GAO testimony GAO-06-961T, dated July 12, 2006. These firms began as small, narrow lenders. By 2006 some ranked among the nation's largest and most complex finance firms.

Between 1987 and 2006, their assets grew over 3,900 percent. The total rose from $3.8 billion to over $155 billion. Trade interest in owning such firms rose with that growth. GAO set out how rules for these lenders differ from rules for like firms. That split in watch, it argued, is the point Congress should grasp as the sector swells.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-971t:
Medicare Part B drug pay, and the price data behind it, is the topic of GAO testimony GAO-06-971T, dated July 13, 2006. The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services sets payments with a price gauge fixed in law, called the average sales price. Deals between buyers vary, so the price each buyer pays can differ.

GAO called the gauge a workable way to set pay, given the limits of other choices. But the agency lacked data it needs to watch payment rates well. Concerns thus remain. The testimony helps readers see how one price average can shape what Medicare pays for costly drugs.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-981t:
Surplus military gear controls get a further GAO airing in testimony GAO-06-981T, dated July 25, 2006, the spoken mate to a report issued the same day. Past GAO work, three testimonies and two reports, had shown lost and stolen sensitive gear. Some of it reached public sale.

Congress asked for fresh probes. GAO tested if outsiders could still obtain gear that must be destroyed once the military is done with it. It checked if new steps stop sales of fresh gear that troops still need or that the department still buys. Control failures still pose a grave security risk, GAO reported, with waste going on.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-991t:
The business case for the F-22A fighter is questioned in GAO testimony GAO-06-991T, dated July 25, 2006. The Air Force jet pairs stealth and sharp turns with new avionics and an engine that cruises past sound without afterburners. Its history shows sharp cost and schedule growth.

Since the program began in 1986, new demands were added and the build span more than doubled. Planned buys fell by more than 75 percent. Unit costs rose by more than 100 percent. The Defense Department sought to buy the last 60 jets on a 3-year deal. GAO gave Congress its views on that plan and the multiyear request.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1021t:
Bills to firm up federal watchdogs are weighed in GAO testimony GAO-07-1021T, dated June 20, 2007. H.R. 928, the Improving Government Accountability Act, would boost inspector general freedom. It would also set up a joint council of those watchdogs.

GAO gave facts and views on the bill's parts, drawn from its past work. It stressed that joint work between GAO and the watchdogs matters more than ever. Fiscal strain and rising program demands drive that need. In May the Comptroller General met the watchdogs to plan closer joint work. The testimony shows two audit arms, and how they can lift each other's reach.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1041t:
One money system for a merged security department stays hard to build, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1041T, dated June 28, 2007. Since 2003 the Department of Homeland Security has tried to join 22 varied agencies. A single finance system would give sound, timely data across them all.

The testimony rests on GAO report GAO-07-536, issued in 2007. GAO summed up the department's finance revamp to date. It drew out the chief hurdles in that revamp. It set out building blocks the department should use as its base. The record shows why merged books are a slow, risky build, even years after a merger.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1051t:
Job training under the Workforce Investment Act could gain from more steps, GAO states in testimony GAO-07-1051T, dated June 28, 2007. The act, passed in 1998, set one-stop centers and training for workers, youth, and the jobless. GAO has reported on it many times since.

The testimony draws on reports from 2000 to 2007. It weighs headway by federal, state, and local staff in putting key parts in place. It names hurdles that block one smooth system for jobs and training. Past advice touched scores, funding splits, centers, and aid for set groups. The statement is a compact tour of a decade of findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1081t:
Four years of the Homeland Security Department are graded in GAO testimony GAO-07-1081T, dated September 6, 2007. The merger ranks among the largest federal reshapes in decades. GAO had called it a huge management test, made more vital by its security role. Such merges can take 5 to 7 years to settle.

The testimony rests on an August 2007 report. GAO tracked the department's headway since March 2003 across 14 mission and management fields. It drew out themes that shaped that record. Readers get a broad scorecard: where a young giant of a department has grown sound, and where it still lags.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1111t:
Use of contractor past performance in federal buying is laid out in GAO testimony GAO-07-1111T, dated July 18, 2007. The government is the world's largest buyer. It obligated over $400 billion in fiscal year 2006. Deals should go only to sound firms, held to account for their work.

GAO set out the ways a firm's past work can count in a buy. It told how past performance facts are meant to guide source choice, and the tools for that use. It named key issues seen in GAO bid protest rulings. Past advice stands, but the testimony adds no new points. It is a clear map of a key buying test.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1121t:
Finishing and keeping up the International Space Station is the strain in GAO testimony GAO-07-1121T, dated July 24, 2007. NASA faces its biggest shift since the moon landings. It must end station assembly with the shuttle, retire the shuttle, and build new craft for future exploration, all at once.

GAO shared early results from work in progress, plus past findings. It set out three hurdles: using the shuttle to finish the station, keeping the shuttle workforce to the end, and filling the gap till new craft can serve the station. How NASA meets them, GAO said, will decide if the station stays a sound research base.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1211t:
Federal technology projects can waste large sums when planning and oversight are weak. This GAO testimony — GAO-07-1211T, presented September 20, 2007 — updates Congress on two watch lists. The Office of Management and Budget flags poorly planned projects on its Management Watch List. Agencies also name high risk projects that may perform poorly. GAO drew on its past reports and current list data.

GAO said about 227 projects had been flagged as poorly planned, poorly performing, or both. Those projects totaled at least $10.4 billion planned for fiscal year 2008. The budget office listed 103 projects as poorly planned, worth about $4.5 billion. Agencies named 91 high risk projects as poorly performing, worth about $1.8 billion. GAO credited some fixes but said the office still does not publish why projects land on the lists.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1221t:
Iraq's leaders had promised laws and security steps meant to pull the country together. In GAO-07-1221T, dated September 5, 2007, GAO testified on how far those promises had gotten. The statement covers the same 18 benchmarks set in a 2007 funding law. GAO rated each benchmark as met, partly met, or not met. Its staff visited Iraq and drew on about 100 earlier GAO products on the war.

The tally was 3 benchmarks met, 4 partly met, and 11 not met as of late August. A late August Unity Accord joined Shi'a, Sunni Arab, and Kurdish leaders. It covered draft laws on de-Ba'athification reform and provincial powers. GAO warned that deep splits among Iraq's groups still blocked real progress. It also questioned how well violence in Baghdad could even be measured.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1241t:
Fusion centers pool police and intelligence data to spot crime and terror threats. GAO gave early findings on these state and local centers in GAO-07-1241T on September 27, 2007. The testimony draws on GAO's draft report on the centers. GAO interviewed officials at 58 centers plus federal homeland security and justice staff. Federal agencies were starting to partner with the centers and share systems with them.

Of the 58 centers, 43 called themselves operational as of September 2007. Thirty-four of those had opened since January 2004. Most centers covered all crimes, not just terrorism. Center officials named real hurdles, GAO reported. Thirty centers struggled with too many systems and heavy, often duplicate, information flows. Others faced trouble meeting security rules for access to federal networks. GAO weighed how far federal help went toward easing those problems.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1251t:
Alaska Native corporations hold special advantages in a federal small business contracting program. GAO explained why those advantages need closer watching in GAO-07-1251T, issued September 19, 2007. The firms may win sole-source contracts of any size under the 8(a) program. They may also own several subsidiaries inside the program. The testimony summed up GAO's earlier report on the trend.

GAO found that oversight had not kept pace with the growth. The Small Business Administration had not tailored its rules to these firms' unique status. Agency contracting staff did not always tell the SBA about contract changes. In one case, an Energy Department officer broadened a contract until its value nearly tripled. Files also showed little proof that firms met rules on doing work with their own staff. GAO urged fixes that the agencies mostly accepted.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-391t:
Taxpayers owed $345 billion more than they paid on time for tax year 2001. GAO laid out the attack plan in testimony GAO-07-391T on January 23, 2007. The tax agency expects to recover $55 billion of the gap. That leaves a net gap of $290 billion. Each 1 percent cut in the net gap yields about $3 billion a year. The testimony weighs three broad approaches. It draws on GAO's prior body of work.

Simplification could cut errors at the source, GAO said. New enforcement tools form the second lever. Reporting the cost basis of stock sales is one example. It would help filers and auditors alike. More enforcement staff form the third lever. Added resources return billions, past work shows. Collection lags vary by taxpayer type. Five years after assessment, 48 percent was collected from business owners. The figure for the largest firms was 97 percent.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-481t: Drug prices in federal programs got a GAO look in 2007, and the briefing examines the oversight of what the government paid for pills. The testimony probes the pricing. The findings ask whether the taxpayer was getting fleeced at the pharmacy.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-491t: Freedom-of-information requests were piling up in 2007, and GAO's briefing says the processing trends showed why improvement plans mattered. The findings track the backlog. The report's creed: the public's right to know should not wait in line. The sunshine law needed more sunshine.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-501t: Kids' health insurance was up for renewal in 2007, and GAO's briefing reviews the states' SCHIP enrollment and spending experience. The testimony previews the reauthorization fight. The findings ask whether the program covering millions of children would survive. The children's coverage hung in the balance.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-551t: Car fuel-economy rules got an early look in 2007, and GAO's briefing offers preliminary notes on the corporate average standards. The testimony previews the coming debate. The findings ask how far a gallon should go, and who gets to decide.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-581t: Catching nuclear smugglers needed better gadgets in 2007, and GAO's briefing questions Homeland Security's plan to buy the next generation of radiation detectors. The testimony probes the procurement. The findings warn that the bomb-sniffing bet had to be right the first time.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-601t: March brought more bad news for the Capitol's basement project in 2007, and GAO's briefing logs the Visitor Center's latest schedule slips and costs. The testimony's refrain stayed grim month after month. The findings kept Congress's microscope fixed on its own money pit.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-661t: Overseas buyers of U.S. firms got a vetting check in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the reviews of foreign deals could be improved. The testimony probes the process in detail. The findings ask whether the gatekeepers were watching the right gates.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-741t: Voting machines were a national headache in 2007 — GAO's briefing says every level of government had to step up to fix the e-voting troubles. The testimony spreads the duty wide. The findings warn that democracy's own machines cannot run on good intentions alone.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-751t: The cyber weak spots would not heal in 2007 — GAO's briefing says persistent holes showed the need for much deeper fixes than patches. The testimony refuses the usual happy talk from officials. The findings' drumbeat is steady: patch the systems, not the press releases.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-821t: School disaster plans were mostly on paper by 2007 — GAO's briefing takes the national temperature of district preparedness. The testimony grades how ready schools really were. The findings' message: a plan in a binder is not a plan in a crisis, and districts needed help to close the gap.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-841t: The rail safety cops were aiming smarter in 2007 — GAO's briefing says the railroad administration targeted risks better but still owed proof of results. The testimony balances credit with caution. The findings demand evidence that the smarter targeting actually saved lives.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-861t: Good teachers were the eternal puzzle in 2007 — GAO's briefing reviews how federal programs tried to build, place, and judge them. The testimony sorts the approaches and the evidence. The findings ask the classroom question that never ages: what makes a teacher great, and can policy make more of them?
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-901t: The watchdog's own house got a diversity check in 2007 — GAO's briefing reports on its drive for a fair and mixed workforce. The testimony practices what the agency preaches to others. The findings show the auditor auditing itself on inclusion, with numbers to back it.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-911t: Body armor math was life-and-death in 2007 — GAO's briefing digs into the Army and Marines' vest requirements, controls, and open questions. The testimony counts the plates and the gaps. The findings ask whether the troops' armor matched the threats.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-991t: Flood payouts after the hurricanes needed a hard audit in 2007 — GAO's briefing gives an early read on whether FEMA paid claims right. The testimony previews the accuracy questions. The findings put the flood insurer's checkbook under the microscope while the waters were still fresh.

gao-gaoreports-gao-08-131t: GAO briefed Congress in 2007 on SBInet — the plan for a high-tech virtual fence along the border. It reads as the first draft of a cautionary tale: a big-ticket border tech bet that would later collapse after burning through cash with little fence to show.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-171t: A 2007 Government Accountability Office testimony marking one year since the SAFE Port Act: a progress report on maritime security reforms. GAO reviews what had been implemented at America's ports — cargo screening, facility security, information sharing — and what was still pending. The testimony measures a landmark law's first year against the threats it was written to counter.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-191t: GAO gave Congress a first progress note in 2007 on the great TV switch — killing old-style broadcasts for digital. Early numbers showed how many homes were ready and how the coupon handout for signal boxes was faring. The briefing offered lawmakers an early taste of the question hanging over the deadline: ready or not?
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-231t: Delivered as 2007 testimony, this Government Accountability Office report summarizes its audits of the effort to secure, stabilize, and rebuild Iraq. Drawing on years of fieldwork, GAO lays out the key oversight issues: wasted reconstruction dollars, unreliable progress measures, and strategic drift. The testimony compresses the watchdog's Iraq findings into a blunt briefing for a Congress losing patience with the war.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-261t: In this 2007 testimony, the Government Accountability Office finds federal telework programs drifting without clear goals or reliable data. Agencies were expanding work-from-home arrangements, but few could say what they were trying to achieve or measure the results. GAO recommends defined objectives and better tracking — advice that looks prescient in light of how central remote work would later become.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-271t: GAO told Congress in 2007 that the VA had spruced up its rules for vetting doctors — who gets to do which procedures — but never checked if clinics followed them. Good rules on paper, no proof in practice. The briefing warns that without spot-checks at the care sites themselves, the new policies were just words in a binder.
